findings.title: [P1] Keep branch arguments out of the shell
findings.body: Any caller-controlled branch value is now interpreted as shell syntax. For example, `HEAD; <command>` executes the appended command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile()` implementation safely passed the branch as a discrete argument.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve cancellation of the Git process
findings.body: `exec()` inserts a shell between the caller and Git. Killing the returned `ChildProcess` can terminate only that shell while leaving a long-running `git show` process alive with inherited output pipes. `execFile()` returned the Git process directly.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve cancellation of the actual Git process
findings.body:
`exec()` inserts a shell between the caller and Git. On POSIX, calling `.kill()` on the returned `ChildProcess` terminates only that shell, potentially leaving a long-running `git show` orphaned and keeping its inherited output pipes open. This breaks cancellation for large objects or slow repositories; `execFile()` previously returned the Git process itself.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argv element instead of shell interpolation
findings.body:
`exec()` invokes a shell, so a branch value such as `main; <command>` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. Git also permits shell metacharacters such as `;` and `$()` in branch names, so valid branch inputs can trigger this. The previous `execFile()` call treated the value as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
